Idempotent Seeding

Deleting everything before recreating it, in the right order, so the seed script is safe to run again and again.

A seed script you can only safely run once against a fresh database is annoying in practice — you'll want to reset your data constantly while building and testing. This project's main() starts by deleting every row, before creating anything:

// Figure 2.12: reset before reseeding (prisma/seed.js, excerpt)
await prisma.notification.deleteMany();
await prisma.ticketWatcher.deleteMany();
await prisma.ticketTag.deleteMany();
await prisma.comment.deleteMany();
await prisma.ticket.deleteMany();
await prisma.tag.deleteMany();
await prisma.user.deleteMany();

A script with this at the top is called idempotent — running it five times in a row leaves the database in exactly the same state as running it once. That property is worth naming because it's not automatic; it comes directly from how this deletes.

The order matters, and it's the opposite of how the tables get created: every foreign key from the schema topics — Ticket.customerId, Comment.ticketId, TicketTag.tagId, and the rest — means MySQL will refuse to delete a row that something else still points to. Deleting notification and the join tables first, then comment and ticket, and user/tag last, guarantees nothing is ever deleted while something else still references it. Creating data afterward runs in the mirror-image order — users and tags first, so their ids exist to be referenced when tickets, comments, and the join rows are created next.
